name: Björn Borg

techniqueNotes.note: Western-leaning grip with a closed-to-square stance and a looped backswing that drops the racquet head well below the ball, then brushes steeply low-to-high and finishes over the opposite shoulder. The heavy topspin gave him huge net clearance with the ball still dipping inside the baseline.

Started the swing with both hands, drove through contact with the hips and shoulders rotating together, then let the top hand release after contact so the finish looked one-handed. This hockey-slapshot release gave extra reach and racquet-head speed while keeping two-handed stability at impact.
Took many small adjustment steps and recovered to the middle immediately after every shot, staying low with a wide base so he was always balanced before swinging.

lesson: Aim high over the net with heavy topspin and recover after every ball: margin plus fitness beats risk.

name: Jimmy Connors

techniqueNotes.note: Hit almost flat with a short, straight-back takeback and a level swing path through the ball, contacting it well out in front on the rise. He stepped into the shot and drove his body weight forward, often leaving the ground, so pace came from the legs and hips rather than the arm.

Stood on or inside the baseline, split-stepped as the server made contact, and used a compact abbreviated swing that redirected the server's pace. Taking the ball early took time away and turned the return into an attacking shot.
Eastern-to-continental grip with a flat, skidding trajectory and very little net clearance. Copy the early preparation and forward weight transfer, but add more topspin than he did for safety.

lesson: Take the ball early with a compact swing and step forward into every return.

name: Guillermo Vilas

techniqueNotes.note: One of the first heavy-topspin one-handers: strong eastern backhand grip, full shoulder turn with the back almost facing the net, and a steep low-to-high swing with a firm wrist that finished high above the head. The non-hitting arm stayed back to keep the shoulders closed through contact.

Big looping lefty forehand brushed up the back of the ball with a relaxed arm, producing a high, heavy ball that pushed opponents behind the baseline. He hit from a loaded back leg and rotated up into the shot.

Popularised the between-the-legs shot (the Gran Willy): chase the lob with the ball dropping in front of you, let it fall to ankle height between the feet, and flick a continental-grip wrist snap through the legs at the last moment.

lesson: Topspin off both wings lets you swing hard and still keep the ball in play all day.

name: John Newcombe

techniqueNotes.note: Continental grip with a heavy, deep second serve that kicked almost as hard as his first, letting him follow both deliveries to the net. He tossed slightly into the court so his momentum carried him forward into the first volley.
Split-stepped around the service line as the returner hit, then punched the first volley deep with a short, firm block and no backswing before closing in for the put-away.
Flat, heavy eastern forehand struck with a firm wrist and a long follow-through toward the target; he ran around second serves to hit it as an approach shot.

lesson: A reliable, deep second serve is what makes an attacking game possible.

name: Ilie Năstase

techniqueNotes.note: Disguised the topspin lob by preparing exactly as for a passing shot, then at the last instant dropped the racquet head and brushed sharply upward with a loose wrist. The identical preparation froze net rushers.
Used a continental grip and a high-to-low carving motion with soft hands, opening the racquet face under the ball at contact and shortening the follow-through to kill the pace.

Known for the over-the-shoulder backhand smash and retrieving shots hit with his back to the net: turn sideways, reach high with a continental grip, and snap the wrist downward rather than swinging the whole arm.

lesson: Disguise comes from preparing every shot the same way and changing only the last moment.

name: Arthur Ashe

techniqueNotes.note: Loose, whippy service motion with a relaxed arm and late wrist snap that produced pace without muscling the ball. In the 1975 Wimbledon final he swung sliced serves wide to the two-hander's backhand to pull the opponent off court.
Could drive the backhand flat or with topspin from a full shoulder turn, releasing the racquet head freely through contact; one of the freest-swinging one-handers of his era.

Took pace off deliberately with low, soft slices and chips down the middle, denying a rhythm hitter the speed and angles he fed on. Keep the face slightly open and swing high-to-low with a long, smooth follow-through.

lesson: Play to a plan: change pace and give opponents the ball they least like rather than the ball you most like.

name: Ken Rosewall

techniqueNotes.note: His backhand was a driven slice: continental grip, early shoulder turn with the racquet head above the hand, and a long, only slightly downward swing through the ball with the face barely open. The result was a fast, low, penetrating ball rather than a floating chip.
Stepped across with the front foot, kept the head still and the non-hitting arm extended behind for balance, and finished with the racquet travelling out toward the target.
Compact and precise: racquet head up, wrist firm, contact in front with a short punch, relying on placement and depth instead of power.

lesson: A slice hit through the ball, not under it, is a weapon that stays low and lasts a lifetime.

name: Stan Smith

techniqueNotes.note: Used his height with full upward extension at contact and a simple, rhythmical motion, tossing in front so his body moved into the court and straight toward the net.
Closed tight to the net behind the serve and volleyed with a firm wrist and minimal backswing, using his reach to cut off passing shots with a crossover step.
Turned sideways immediately, pointed at the ball with the free hand, and moved back with side-steps so he could hit the overhead with the same continental-grip motion as the serve.

lesson: Keep attacking mechanics simple and repeatable: reach up, move forward, punch the volley.

name: Vitas Gerulaitis

techniqueNotes.note: Exceptionally quick hands at net: kept the racquet in front of the body with a continental grip and met the ball early with a short block, angling volleys away instead of hitting them hard.
Among the fastest movers of his time; he approached behind almost anything and relied on a well-timed split step and explosive first step to cover the net.
Chipped the backhand approach low and deep down the line while moving through the shot, so the ball stayed low and he was already closing to the net as it bounced.

lesson: Quick feet and a well-timed split step make average volleys into winning ones.

name: Roscoe Tanner

techniqueNotes.note: Hit the ball off a very low toss, striking it at or just before the peak with a fast, compact motion. The low toss gave returners little time to read the serve and made it reliable in wind, but it demands a quick, well-timed arm.
Generated pace from a strong knee bend and rapid shoulder rotation rather than a long wind-up, with the lefty slice swinging wide in the ad court to open the court for the first volley.
Followed the flat serve in and looked to finish with the first or second volley, keeping points short and volleys directed into the open court.

lesson: A lower, consistent toss and a fast compact motion can add disguise and rhythm to your serve.

name: Chris Evert

techniqueNotes.note: Early unit turn with both hands on the grip, a compact straight takeback, and a level swing through a contact point just in front of the lead hip. Her head stayed still and she finished with both hands up by the opposite shoulder, which made the stroke repeatable under pressure.
Flat-to-mild-topspin eastern forehand hit with a firm wrist, early preparation and a long follow-through toward the target, prioritising depth and placement within a metre of the lines.
Against net rushers she used the same preparation as her passing shot, then lifted a deep lob over the backhand side, forcing the volleyer to respect both options.

lesson: Early preparation and a still head give you the consistency that wins more matches than power.

name: Billie Jean King

techniqueNotes.note: Attacked the net relentlessly, moving diagonally forward through each volley so her body weight, not a swing, supplied the pace. She stayed low with bent knees on low volleys and kept the racquet head above the wrist.
Her backhand was her stronger wing: a sliced or flat drive hit with a full shoulder turn, used as an approach shot she followed straight to the net.
Turned sideways at once and retreated with crossover steps, keeping the ball in front of the hitting shoulder so she could hit a confident overhead and hold her net position.

lesson: Move forward through your volleys and let your legs do the work.

name: Evonne Goolagong Cawley

techniqueNotes.note: Fluid one-hander she could slice, drive or roll with topspin from the same relaxed preparation, with a loose arm and a long, unhurried follow-through. The backhand volley in particular was hit with a smooth carve and soft hands.
Glided to the ball with light, balanced steps and arrived early, so she rarely looked rushed; smooth movement let her swing freely instead of compensating with the arm.
Natural touch at net: absorbed pace with a relaxed grip and angled volleys short, choosing placement and feel over force.

lesson: Relaxed arms and balanced movement produce effortless timing.

name: Margaret Court

techniqueNotes.note: Used her height and long reach with full extension at contact and followed the serve in, relying on pioneering strength and fitness training to hold the attacking pattern for entire matches.
Her exceptional arm span let her cut off passing shots with one crossover step; she volleyed firmly with a short punch and closed the net to shrink the angles.
Athletic overhead hit with a serve-like motion and a strong leg drive, which made lobbing her an unreliable escape.

lesson: Physical conditioning is technique's foundation: strength and reach make an attacking game sustainable.

name: Virginia Wade

techniqueNotes.note: One of the best serves in the women's game of her time: a high toss, deep knee bend and full shoulder rotation with a continental grip, producing a first serve she could follow to the net.
Sliced backhand approach hit with a high-to-low carve and a forward step through the ball, kept low and deep so she could close in behind it.
Aggressive first volley hit with forward momentum and a firm wrist, aimed deep to the open court to set up an easier second volley.

lesson: Build the point around a confident serve and a low approach shot.

name: Rosie Casals

techniqueNotes.note: At 5 ft 2 in she compensated with speed and anticipation, closing very tight to the net and taking volleys early and high with quick, acrobatic reactions and a compact punch.
Despite her height she had a fearless overhead, jumping with a scissor kick to reach lobs and hitting with a full serve-like motion.
Explosive first step and constant small adjustment steps allowed her to cover the net and recover for the next ball, proving court coverage can offset a lack of reach.

lesson: Quickness, anticipation and courage at net matter more than height.

name: Kerry Melville Reid

techniqueNotes.note: Classic Australian eastern forehand: side-on stance, racquet taken back early, and a smooth swing with weight moving from back foot to front foot through a contact point level with the front hip.
Steady sliced backhand hit with a continental grip and long follow-through, used to keep the ball low on grass and to approach the net.

lesson: Sound, simple fundamentals and weight transfer hold up on every surface.

name: Sue Barker

techniqueNotes.note: Her forehand was the dominant weapon of her game: a big shoulder turn, a fast whipping swing and contact well out in front, hit with far more pace than was normal in the women's game of the 1970s.
Ran around the backhand to hit inside-out forehands, using quick side-steps to create space from the ball so she could take a full swing from her stronger side.
Protected the weaker wing with a safe sliced backhand kept deep, buying time until she could get a forehand.

lesson: Build your game around your best shot and use your feet to hit it as often as possible.

name: Wendy Turnbull

techniqueNotes.note: Nicknamed Rabbit for her speed: a low centre of gravity, fast small steps and immediate recovery toward the middle let her retrieve balls others conceded.
A world-class doubles player, she volleyed with a compact punch and good positioning, moving forward through the ball and aiming at the feet or the gaps.
Chipped the backhand low and approached behind it, keeping the racquet face stable and the follow-through extended toward the target.

lesson: Relentless footwork and recovery can take a player to Grand Slam finals.

name: Mima Jaušovec

techniqueNotes.note: A clay-court specialist who slid into her shots, planting the outside foot and sliding so she was balanced at contact and could push straight back to the centre.
Used the drop shot from the baseline to break baseline rhythm on clay, disguising it with normal groundstroke preparation and an open-faced, softened contact.
Steady one-handed backhand played with height and depth over the net, favouring margin and patience over outright winners.

lesson: On clay, patience, depth and variety win points without needing big power.
